# Ozal

> Ozal is an open-source, self-hosted access gateway. One Go binary puts a
> sign-in and per-route policy in front of internal web apps, so people can
> reach them without a VPN.

Ozal terminates HTTPS, identifies each visitor with a passkey or an OIDC
provider, applies the route's rules, and only then forwards the request to the
application. It is a reverse proxy, an identity front door and a policy
decision point for self-hosted software. It is not a VPN, not an identity
provider, and it does not replace an application's own authorization.

- Status: early alpha. Interfaces and configuration may change; release
  downloads are not published yet.
- License: MIT.
- Written in Go; one binary for Linux, macOS and Windows.
- Source: https://github.com/ozal-project/ozal
- Project page: https://ozal.dev/

## What it does

- Routes by hostname to an HTTP app or a static site, with health checks.
- Issues and renews TLS certificates; each domain has its own certificate.
- Signs people in with passkeys or an existing OIDC provider.
- Applies per-route policy (people, groups, email domains, recent sign-in,
  device-bound passkey) and returns a stable decision code and reason.
- Strips client-supplied identity headers, injects the authenticated identity
  for the app, and never forwards the session cookie.
- Shows every access decision with its code and reason in the console; a
  durable audit trail is available when configured.
- Publishes static sites from GitHub Actions with deployment history and
  one-step rollback.

## What it does not do

- It does not replace a VPN for arbitrary TCP or UDP traffic.
- It does not replace the application's own permissions: Ozal decides who
  reaches the app, not what they do inside it.
- It is not a commercial product and has no hosted service.
- It is not production-ready: this is an early alpha used on the author's
  server.

## Similar tools

If you know Cloudflare Access or Pomerium, Ozal is the same idea — an access
gateway in front of self-hosted apps — on a server you own, as one Go binary.
Unlike a hosted service, it needs no cloud account, and it can run behind a
proxy or directly on the host.

## Questions it answers

- How do I put an internal app on the internet without a VPN?
- How do I add passkey login to a self-hosted app without changing the app?
- How do I give each app its own access rule and see why a request was allowed
  or refused?
- How do I publish a static site with history and rollback from my own server?
